commits.pr_title: [ROCm][Perf] Parallelise AITER MLA page-index expansion over token chunks
commits.pr_body:
> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Scope: this is a kernel-level microbenchmark, not an end-to-end throughput claim.**
> The numbers below are measured from torch-profiler traces on the same build, same shapes. Against a multi-millisecond decode step a
> change of this size sits inside run-to-run variation (~1% on a conc=1 arm), so
> **no measurable serving throughput improvement is claimed, and none should be
> inferred.** The value is removing a serial per-request loop on a path that is
> on the critical path at low concurrency. Details under "End-to-end context".

## Purpose

`_expand_page_indices_kernel` in the AITER MLA backend is launched with a grid
of one program per request, and each program walks that request's tokens in a
serial loop:

```python
_expand_page_indices_kernel[(num_reqs,)](...)

    req_idx = tl.program_id(0)
    for i in tl.range(0, num_tokens, BLOCK_SIZE):
```

The parallelism is therefore entirely over the batch. That is fine at high
concurrency and degenerates at low concurrency: with `num_reqs == 1` a **single
workgroup** expands the whole sequence while the rest of the GPU idles. The
bug is invisible in the regime it was presumably tuned for.

On a long-context decode workload (MI355X, TP8, ~97k-token context, conc=1)
this measured **61.6 µs per call and 7 calls per model step — 0.431 ms, or
1.23% of a 34.9 ms step**. For scale, 97k int32 stores is ~388 KB, well under
a microsecond of HBM bandwidth. The kernel is not bandwidth-bound; it is
serialised.

This affects **any MLA model on ROCm at low concurrency**, not one model in
particular.

## The change

Add a second grid dimension over token chunks and drop the loop, so each
program handles exactly one `BLOCK_SIZE` chunk:

```python
num_chunks = max(1, cdiv(block_table.shape[1] * kernel_block_size, 1024))
_expand_page_indices_kernel[(num_reqs, num_chunks)](...)
```

The arithmetic, the masks and the stores are unchanged — only the iteration
space is mapped onto the GPU instead of onto one workgroup. The chunk count is
derived host-side from the block table width, an upper bound on tokens per
request, so **no device synchronisation is introduced**; over-launched
programs mask out entirely and cost nothing.

## Not a duplicate

Checked before opening:

```
repo:vllm-project/vllm is:pr is:open expand_page_indices      -> 0 results
```

No open PR touches this kernel or its launch. The nearby open ROCm MLA PRs
address unrelated concerns:

| PR | subject | overlap |
|---|---|---|
| #57085 | ROCM_AITER_MLA non-causal DSpark draft under DCP | none — DCP draft path |
| #53492 | sparse MLA Gluon kernel from Aiter | none — sparse kernel |
| #57923 | startup OOM in AITER MLA FP8 prefill workspace sizing | none — allocation sizing |
| #46172 | optimize rocm aiter sparse mla indexer | none — sparse indexer |
| #54899 | pad the AITER MLA decode head count to a native tile | none — head padding |

The kernel was introduced in #39616 (AITER MLA + Eagle3 on ROCm) and has not
been modified since.

## Test plan

**Bit-exactness against the existing serial kernel.** Both versions built from
source and compared on device — this is an index computation, so a wrong value
does not crash, it silently reads the wrong KV:

```
conc=1 long context, kbs=1    97000 indices identical
conc=1 long context, kbs=16   97000 indices identical
exact multiple of 1024         4096 indices identical
1024+1                         1025 indices identical
1024-1                         1023 indices identical
ragged 4 reqs                 38011 indices identical
kbs=16 ragged tail             4212 indices identical
single token                      1 indices identical
```

Cases cover chunk boundaries, ragged multi-request batches, and
`kernel_block_size > 1`.

### Kernel time — the direct measurement

This is what the change does, measured on the kernel itself rather than
inferred from an end-to-end delta. Torch-profiler traces, same build, same
workload, same serve config, six captured iterations each:

| | calls | total | **µs/call** | per step |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline | 18 | 0.402 ms | **22.4** | 0.067 ms |
| this PR | 18 | 0.059 ms | **3.3** | 0.010 ms |
| | | | **−85.4%** | |

**6.8× faster.** Identical call counts on both sides, so this is the same work
at the same frequency, no longer serialised onto a single workgroup. That is
the claim this PR rests on, and it is reproducible on any machine with a
profiler — it does not depend on our hardware, our workload mix, or run-to-run
variance.

Measured with `vllm serve --profiler-config.profiler=torch`, ISL 131072,
conc=1, TP8, MTP depth 6.

### Concurrency sweep — does the extra grid dimension cost anything?

Requested during review: the win above is at conc=1, where one workgroup walked
the whole context. At higher concurrency `num_reqs` already supplies
parallelism, so the question is whether the second grid dimension costs
anything there.

The kernel grid-strides rather than partitioning, so a grid width of 1
reproduces the pre-PR launch exactly. "Before" below is therefore the same
kernel launched the old way, not a reimplementation. Width is this PR's
launch-site formula, `num_chunks = max(1, cdiv(block_table.shape[1] * kernel_block_size, 1024))`
(an upper bound on tokens per request read from the block-table width, so
it needs no device sync; at `kernel_block_size=1` this gives 375 / 64 / 8 / 1
for the contexts below). MI355X, 256
CUs, `kernel_block_size=1`, `BLOCK_SIZE=1024`, median of 7 reps x 100
iterations on an idle node. Output compared byte-for-byte at every width and
shape; all agree.

| ctx | reqs | width | before µs | after µs | ratio |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 024 | 1 | 1 | 10.99 | 10.95 | 1.00x |
| 1 024 | 256 | 1 | 10.59 | 10.76 | 0.98x |
| 8 192 | 64 | 8 | 10.73 | 10.74 | 1.00x |
| 8 192 | 256 | 8 | 10.78 | 10.74 | 1.00x |
| 65 536 | 1 | 64 | 16.59 | 10.75 | 1.54x |
| 65 536 | 64 | 64 | 25.94 | 10.83 | 2.40x |
| 65 536 | 256 | 64 | 39.69 | 39.54 | 1.00x |
| 384 000 | 1 | 375 | 114.14 | 10.78 | 10.59x |
| 384 000 | 32 | 375 | 137.30 | 28.28 | 4.85x |
| 384 000 | 64 | 375 | 251.07 | 68.34 | 3.67x |
| 384 000 | 128 | 375 | 300.51 | 153.84 | 1.95x |

**No shape regresses.** The lowest ratio anywhere is 0.98x, on shapes sitting
at a ~10.7 µs floor where run-to-run spread is around ±2%. At 1k context the
width is 1, so the launch is bit-identical to before and those rows measure
noise rather than a change.

Ragged batches are the case worth checking explicitly, since
`num_token_blocks` comes from `max_seq_len` over the whole batch — one long
request widens the grid for every short request too, launching programs that
find nothing to do:

| batch | width | before µs | after µs | ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1x384k + 7x1k | 375 | 115.60 | 10.86 | 10.64x |
| 1x384k + 63x1k | 375 | 115.67 | 13.80 | 8.38x |
| 1x65k + 127x512 | 64 | 16.62 | 10.74 | 1.55x |
| 8x65k + 56x1k | 64 | 17.01 | 10.80 | 1.58x |

The widened grid costs nothing measurable: 63 short requests at width 375 still
come out 8.4x ahead, because the programs with no work exit immediately.

Ratios converging to 1.00x at the high end (65k/256) are the expected
behaviour rather than a cost — the "before" side has enough requests to fill
the machine on its own. These remain kernel microbenchmarks; at high
concurrency this kernel is a small share of the step, so the table is here to
show the change does not cost anything there, not to claim a win.

### End-to-end context

The kernel runs 3 times per step on current main, so the 0.057 ms it saves is
about **0.24%** of a 23.40 ms step. That is below what a 1200 s conc=1 arm can
resolve, and it is the honest ceiling for this change on this configuration.

Earlier end-to-end arms are included for completeness, but should **not** be
read as the effect size:

| build | | interactivity p90 | tpot p90 | step time |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | baseline | 110.28 | 0.00907 | 34.01 ms |
| A | this PR | 112.06 (+1.61%) | 0.00892 | 33.45 ms |
| B | baseline | 140.97 | 0.00709 | 26.59 ms |
| B | this PR | 142.75 (+1.27%) | 0.00701 | 26.29 ms |

Both figures exceed what the kernel can physically save, so they are
noise-dominated at this effect size — a 1200 s conc=1 arm carries roughly 1%
run-to-run spread, against a ceiling here well under that. A third arm on
current main measured −0.35%, which is the same noise in the other direction.
The kernel measurement above is the reliable signal; these rows are not.

Worth noting why the end-to-end impact shrank across builds: the per-call cost
is essentially unchanged (23.3 µs then, 22.4 µs now), but upstream reduced the
call count from 6 per step to 3. The serialisation this PR removes is the same;
there is simply less of it to remove than there was.

**Accuracy** is unaffected by construction — the page indices are bit-
identical, so the model reads exactly the same KV. Confirmed anyway with
GSM8k over the full 1319 questions: 0.9659, unchanged.

## AI assistance

AI assistance was used for this PR (Claude). The measurements above are from
runs on real hardware, not estimates. The submitter has reviewed every changed
line.

## Purpose

This fix changes masked scale data from 127 (value 1.0 for e8m0) to 0 (value 2^(-127). This change is benign in terms of accuracy as the main value side already loads corresponding lanes for mfma as 0. So, scales get multiplied by 0 and has no accuracy effect.

When other=127, triton 3.8.0+gitc0a142ff leads to reading stale LDS data for the lanes corresponding to the masked scales due to a compiler bug. This bug is fixed on upstream triton but this fix resolves stale data reading issue for both compiler versions.

With other=127 and triton 3.8.0+gitc0a142ff, if LDS addresses corresponding to the masked lanes have "NaN", this leads to the result and produce inaccurate results. This is a rare case but it can still happen in practice. Reproduction relies on what LDS contains from previous runs.

This is a cleaner solution as hardware can already handle writing 0s to the masked lanes almost for free compared to writing any other value.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Frontend] Check reused prompt token ids against the vocab before streaming
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Follow-up to #55771, from @NickLucche's review: check that the reused `kv_transfer_params["prompt_token_ids"]` are inside the vocabulary when the prompt is rendered.

Today only `InputProcessor._validate_model_input` checks the vocab bound. With `stream=true` it runs after the stream is returned, so an out-of-vocabulary reused id comes back as an error event inside a 200 response, and `_with_kv_transfer_rejection_cleanup` does not notify the KV connector. The prefill KV then stays held until its lease expires.

Changes:

- `vllm/renderers/base.py`: the engine's vocab check moves into `BaseRenderer.validate_token_ids(token_ids, *, parameter=None)`. The bound (`max(tokenizer.max_token_id, model_vocab_size - 1)`), the negative-id check, the error messages and the "skipped without a tokenizer" rule are unchanged.
- `vllm/v1/engine/input_processor.py`: `_validate_model_input` calls `self.renderer.validate_token_ids(prompt_ids)`. Behaviour is unchanged for generate, embedding and pooling requests.
- `vllm/renderers/online_renderer.py`: `_reused_prompt_token_ids` calls the same helper after its malformed-id check, with `parameter="kv_transfer_params.prompt_token_ids"`. The 400 is raised at render time inside `_with_kv_transfer_rejection_cleanup`, so no stream is opened and the connector is notified, the same path #55771 exercised on a NIXL 1P1D setup for malformed ids. This covers chat (HF and Harmony) and non-Harmony `/v1/responses`.

One helper means the engine and the renderer check cannot drift apart. It is independent of #59491, which fixes `max_token_id` itself; the test uses id 999999.

Not changed: other checks that only run in the engine (for example `bad_words` ids, or out-of-vocab ids in a `/v1/completions` token prompt) still fail after the stream opens under `stream=true`, without notifying the connector. A general fix would notify on pre-admission rejection in `AsyncLLM.generate`; I'm happy to do that separately.

I found no open PR for this.

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest -v tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_serving_chat.py -k kv_transfer_prompt_token_ids
pytest -v tests/entrypoints/openai/responses/test_serving_responses.py tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_batched_chat_completions.py -k kv_transfer
pytest -v tests/test_request_input_bounds.py
pytest -v tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_serving_chat.py tests/entrypoints/openai/responses/test_serving_responses.py
pytest -v tests/entrypoints/llm/test_prompt_validation.py tests/entrypoints/openai/completion/test_prompt_validation.py tests/v1/sample/test_sampling_params_e2e.py
pytest -v tests/entrypoints/pooling/embed/test_online.py -k "negative or vocab or invalid"
```

`test_chat_kv_transfer_prompt_token_ids_rejection_notifies_kv_connector` gains an out-of-vocab case with `stream=true`, which fails without this change.

## Test Result

1x NVIDIA A10G, torch 2.13, this diff on main 51048b13ce.

- Chat reuse tests: 21 passed. Responses and batch reuse tests: 7 passed. `tests/test_request_input_bounds.py`: 39 passed.
- Full `test_serving_chat.py` and `test_serving_responses.py`, engine path (`LLM` and completion prompt validation, sampling-params e2e) and embeddings negative id: 249, 62 and 1 passed on the first revision of this change. The source is unchanged since; review only folded two new tests into the existing one.
- With the render-time call removed, the new out-of-vocab case fails.
- `pre-commit` ruff-check, ruff-format, typos, check-spdx-header and `mypy-3.10`: passed.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Tie lm_head.weight for Nemotron Parse when checkpoint omits it
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Fixes #53019.

`nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-Parse-2.0`'s checkpoint does not materialize a separate
`lm_head.weight` tensor — its config sets `tie_word_embeddings=True` and the
output head is tied to `decoder.embed_tokens.weight` instead (the same convention
the model's Transformers reference implementation follows).

`NemotronParseForConditionalGeneration.load_weights` had no fallback for this:
`self.lm_head` was only ever populated inside the `is_lm_head(name)` branch, which
requires a weight name starting with `"lm_head"` to be present in the checkpoint.
Since that name never appears for this model, `self.lm_head` silently stayed at
its random `nn.Module` init — no error, no warning, no unloaded-weights report.
The server boots and serves requests normally, but every response is garbage.

This PR adds a tied-embeddings fallback: after `load_weights` processes the
encoder/decoder/lm_head weights, if `tie_word_embeddings` is set on the config
(or the decoder sub-config) and no `lm_head.*` weight was seen in the checkpoint,
it ties `self.lm_head.weight = self.decoder.embed_tokens.weight`.

## Test Plan

Manual repro against `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1-ubuntu2404`:

```bash
vllm serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-Parse-2.0 \
    --dtype bfloat16 --max-num-seqs 8 \
    --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": 1}' \
    --trust-remote-code --port 8000
```

Sent a real document image through `/v1/chat/completions` with the model's
documented control-token prompt (`</s><s><predict_bbox><predict_classes><output_markdown>`).

## Test Result

**Before:** fluent-looking but semantically meaningless output interleaved with
stray `<x_...>`/`<y_...>` bbox tokens, unrelated to the input document.

**After:** correct structured markdown output in the model's documented format
(`<x_left><y_top>text<x_right><y_bottom><class_ClassName>`), matching the input
document's actual content. Reproduced on two independent real document images.

Also verified equivalent behavior against the model's own runtime monkeypatch
workaround (`vllm_tied_patch/sitecustomize.py`, shipped in the model's HF repo) —
this PR produces byte-for-byte identical corrected output, folding that
downstream workaround into `load_weights` directly.
